activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Jeremy had signed up to be a peer health educator mostly because the training counted for service hours and because Priya Raman had signed up too, and he was not proud of the arithmetic, but there it was. On the first Tuesday of training, Ms. Okafor handed out a plastic bin of demonstration kits and told them they would learn to explain consent, contraception, and clinic testing well enough to teach it to freshmen. "You will be asked questions you cannot answer," she said. "Practice saying 'I don't know, but I know who does.'" That sentence alone felt worth the whole hour.

The second Tuesday was held in the empty seminar room with the good chairs, and a nurse from the county clinic came with a rolling suitcase that clattered like a fish cart. Her name was Dee. She spread out brochures in fans, burnishing each one flat with the heel of her hand as though the creases were personal insults. Then she had them pair off and role-play. Jeremy drew Marcus Wei, who folded his arms and announced, in the voice of a difficult freshman, "I feel fine, so why would I go get tested for anything?"

Jeremy opened his mouth and closed it. He had been about to say something about being responsible, which he understood instantly would sound like a poster. Dee drifted over, not to rescue him, just to listen with her arms crossed. "Here's the thing," Jeremy tried instead. "You could still have something." Marcus, staying in character, said feeling fine was proof enough for him. Jeremy faltered, and Dee crouched beside their chairs. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms at all," she said. "Testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." Then she straightened up and walked away, leaving the sentence sitting between them like a coin someone had dropped.

Marcus broke character. "Wait, seriously? None?" Jeremy shrugged, but the fact had already rearranged something in his head, the way a hallway looks different after you learn there's a room behind the wall. He thought of his cousin Daniel, who two years ago had sworn up and down that he was clean because he felt clean, the way people swear a car is fine because it starts. Daniel had ended up at a clinic anyway, in March, for reasons nobody in the family would state out loud at Thanksgiving. Jeremy had been fifteen and had not asked a single question.

The role-play went on. Priya, across the room, was handling her freshman with a kind of brisk comedy, miming a condom package instructions leaflet like a flight attendant, and Jeremy laughed despite himself. When it was his turn to play the reluctant student, he made himself truly obnoxious, drawling, "But I feel amazing," until Priya's partner, Sasha, laughed so hard she had to put her head on the table. Dee let the noise run itself out. "Good," she said. "If you can survive this room, you can survive a freshman who thinks he's immortal."

At the end, Ms. Okafor asked each of them to say one thing they would carry into the presentations. Priya said something about the clinic's walk-in hours. Marcus said, to Jeremy's surprise, "The no symptoms thing. That one's going to stick with people." Jeremy had been planning to say something more abstract, about listening before informing, which he privately suspected was an encapsulation of everything he'd absorbed in two Tuesdays, but the word felt too polished for the room, so he abandoned it at the last second and said, "Say 'I don't know, but I know who does.' It actually works." Ms. Okafor nodded like she'd already known that.

Walking out, he caught up with Marcus by the water fountain. "You argued pretty hard in there," Jeremy said. "For a fake freshman." Marcus drank for a long time. "My brother," he said finally, "spent a year feeling fine." He didn't add anything, and Jeremy didn't ask, because some things you leave where they're set down. The hallway smelled like floor wax and somebody's microwaved lunch, and outside the windows the November light had gone the color of dishwater, capricious enough that it might storm or might turn gold within the hour.

Jeremy thought about Daniel again, on the bus home, and about how he'd never once said the word clinic in that house, and about whether honesty was a duty you owed family or a presumption. He didn't land anywhere. He took out his notebook and wrote, "feeling fine is not proof," and underlined it twice, then added a question mark, because he was seventeen and had learned just enough to know that certainty was usually somebody else's confidence borrowed without permission.

The following Tuesday, Ms. Okafor scheduled the first real presentation for December, ninth graders, forty minutes, no co-teacher. She asked for a volunteer. Priya's hand went up fast as a shutter. Jeremy's went up a half second later, and he kept it there.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The line outside the food bank reached the corner of the parking lot before the doors opened at ten. Eva stood behind a folding table stacked with canned tomatoes and wondered whether she should have chosen a Saturday, when she imagined the volunteers would outnumber the visitors. A woman in a lanyard named Priya handed her a clipboard and said, "You take names and household sizes, I bag." The first man through the door gave his name in a voice so quiet Eva had to lean over the table.

By eleven her handwriting had gone small and cramped. A boy from her school, Daniel, came through with his younger sister, and they both pretended not to recognize each other, which was a courtesy she understood and accepted. He counted for a household of four. After he left, Priya glanced at the line still folded along the wall and said, "It's a Tuesday. You'd think a Tuesday would be slower."

Eva looked it up on her phone during her break, crouched beside the milk cooler. Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 had recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. She read the sentence twice. A record for a single month. She had expected the number to be large, but not a record, and she had not expected the record to be now, in an ordinary month with no holiday and no crisis she could name. She sat with the milk sweating against her knee and felt the fact ferment in her, slow and sour, changing shape the longer she held it.

Her mother had sent her here with an injunction she had repeated at the door: be useful, stay quiet, don't stare. Her civics teacher, on the other hand, had spent a unit on structural causes, poverty as a design flaw rather than a personal one, and had told them that charity could soothe the conscience without fixing anything. Eva had written that in an essay and gotten an A. Standing at the table, she found the two positions did not fit together the way they had on paper. Handing a man a bag of rice was not nothing. It was also not enough, and both of those things were true at once, and she could not make them into one sentence.

At noon a volunteer named Gerald, older and obdurate about procedure, refused a woman a second bag of formula because the sheet said one per household per visit. The woman said her sister and the baby were waiting in the car and were a separate household. Gerald said the sheet didn't say that. Priya came over and put her hand flat on the clipboard and said, "Write it as two households. I'll initial it." Gerald's jaw worked, but he stepped back, and Eva wrote the second entry while the woman held her sister's ID against the table edge to keep it steady.

Eva discovered that she had opinions about the clipboard. Rules existed so the supply lasted, and the supply had to last, because there were 2.2 million visits in a single month and this was only one food bank on one Tuesday. But the rules were written somewhere else, by people who had not seen the sister waiting in the car. Priya's initials were a small, local correction, the kind Eva's teacher would probably call a bandage. Eva was not sure the teacher was wrong. She was also not sure that mattered to the woman walking out with the formula, whose problem today was not structural.

Daniel came back near closing because his sister had left her scarf on a chair. He stood at the table while Eva looked for it under the coat rack, and he said, "You can't tell anyone, right." It was not really a question. She found the scarf, gray with a hole at one end, and held it out.

"I won't," she said. She signed out on the volunteer sheet, wrote her hours, and noticed her hand was still cramped from the morning's names. Priya called from the doorway that Tuesday next week she should come early, before the line reaches the corner. Eva zipped her jacket and said, "I'll be here at nine thirty."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
Lucas arrived at the community center twenty minutes early, notebook against his chest, because Ms. Ferreira had offered the only extra credit she offered all semester: attend the town hall on the county charter question and transcribe the public comments verbatim for the school paper. He found a folding chair near the back, third row, where he could see both the podium and the exit. The room smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and a fan in the corner turned its head slowly, like it was deciding whom to blame.

The meeting opened with the Pledge, then a budget item about the firehouse roof, then the charter amendment itself. When the moderator called for questions, a woman at the microphone said the whole thing felt rigged, like some foreign parliament where nobody votes for anything directly. Lucas's pencil stopped. He was supposed to be neutral, a transcription machine, but his own government class was swimming in his head, and he wanted, suddenly and badly, to be the one who answered her.

He got his chance in the lobby afterward, at a folding table where volunteers handed out voter registration forms. A girl from the college, tabling for a civic engagement club, had been explaining something to an older man in a gravel trucker cap, and Lucas drifted close enough to hear. "So they got a king over there," the man said, "and a prime minister under him? What's the king for, then, decoration?"

"Basically," the girl said. "In a lot of parliamentary systems the head of state is separate from the head of government. The monarch or the ceremonial president does the ribbon cuttings and the prime minister actually runs things." She tapped her stack of forms square. "In the United States our president is both."

Lucas had written a paper two weeks ago claiming the opposite, that a prime minister was just a president with a British accent, and Ms. Ferreira had marked it with a single question mark that he had not followed up on. The question mark had been sitting in his folder since, half shame and half splinter. Now the splinter moved. He waited until the gravel man took his form and left, then stepped up to the table.

"I got that backwards on a paper," he said. "I said the prime minister and the king were the same office in different centuries."

The girl laughed, not unkindly. "Half my intro class did too, first week."

"Is there a way to test which I actually understand," Lucas asked, "besides writing it again and hoping?" He explained about the town hall, the transcript, the woman who thought anything parliamentary was rigged. He asked whether he could quote the exchange at her table. She said that depended on its veracity, which he should check somewhere better than a folding table, and slid a thin blue textbook across it. "Chapter four. Borrow it, bring it back to the next meeting."

He sat on the curb outside with the book while the parking lot emptied, headlights sweeping the brick face of the firehouse. Chapter four laid the two systems side by side, and what struck him was not the diagram but the removal part: a parliament could withdraw its confidence and the head of government was gone, sometimes inside a week, while here a president served out the term unless the whole cumbersome machinery of impeachment turned over. One made it easy to fire the boss and hard to know who'd be next; the other made the boss nearly immovable and the succession perfectly predictable. He had always assumed predictability was the obvious good. Now he wasn't sure which he'd choose if the choice were his, and the not-sure felt less like failure than like the room had gotten bigger.

Inside, the cleanup crew was stacking chairs, and Ms. Ferreira was zipping her bag by the door. She saw the blue book on his knees. "You followed the question mark," she said.

"I got it wrong first," Lucas said. "Then a girl at the registration table, she's from the college, she set me straight, and I'm not done deciding which system I'd actually defend." He stood. "The woman who called it rigged, in there. Part of what bothered her is that in the parliamentary version you never vote for the head of government directly, and part of what bothers me about our version is the opposite. I can argue both sides now. That's new."

Ms. Ferreira looked at him for a long moment, the fan still turning its slow head behind her. "Then write that," she said, "the both-sides version, with the transcript attached," and held the door open.

Outside, the October air had gone cold and the last car's exhaust hung white under the streetlight. Lucas tucked the blue book under his arm where he wouldn't drop it, took out his phone, and typed a note to himself: return book, next meeting. Then, underneath, still standing in the emptying lot, he added a second line and read it back to himself aloud: "Ask her name."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: The Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.
story:
The article was four paragraphs long, in Spanish, and Isabella had read the first paragraph six times before the words stopped sliding off her. She sat in the far corner of the school library where the carrels faced the window, her phone face down beside a dictionary she was trying not to open. The piece was from a Chilean paper: the port authority in Valparaíso wanted to expropriate a strip of hillside houses to widen a cargo corridor, and the city council had split over it. She had volunteered for this. Five minutes, in Spanish, in front of the whole class on Thursday, arguing one side and then summarizing the article aloud. Her teacher had said the word "B2" when she assigned it, and Isabella had nodded as if she knew what that meant.

She did not know what that meant. She copied the first sentence into her notebook, then underlined every verb she recognized. Queria. Expropiar. She looked up long enough to see Dana from her class slide into the opposite carrel, drop a binder, and start highlighting something with the concentration of a person performing concentration.

"Ask your phone," Dana said, without looking up.

"I'm not asking my phone."

"You asked your phone for the debate topic."

Isabella turned the phone over. The course outline was in her email, a PDF her teacher had sent in September, and she had never scrolled past the second page. She scrolled now. Under "Trimestre 3" it said, in English, that students at B2 level should be able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. She read it twice. It didn't say argue. It didn't say win. It said explain, and it wanted both sides, advantages and disadvantages, laid out.

"That's it?" Dana leaned across the aisle. "That's all B2 is?"

"That's what the outline says." She turned the screen so Dana could see it.

"So you don't need to beat Tomas. You just need to sound like you read the article."

Isabella pulled the screen back. She had been planning to beat Tomas. Tomas had spent a semester in Madrid and rolled his r's like a native, and she had spent a semester ordering the wrong sandwich at the deli on Fulton Street. She had planned to memorize a script so dense he couldn't get a word in.

She read the second paragraph again. The port handled more cargo than the rail line could carry; a city planner was quoted saying the throughput of the corridor had to double or the shipping companies would move to San Antonio. Throughput. Rendimiento. Even in English the word was a kind of wall. She wrote "throughput" in her notebook and drew an arrow to a house.

Because the third paragraph was the houses. Eleven of them. A woman named Rosa Herrera had lived in hers for forty years, and the compensation offer covered the market price and nothing else, and her street was the only one where the fishermen still repaired nets outside in the evenings. The reporter didn't editorialize. The reporter gave the planner his numbers and gave Rosa her sentence about nets, and then the article ended.

Isabella tried out the summary in a whisper. "El puerto quiere expropiar las casas." Her accent flattened every vowel. She tried it again, louder than she meant to, and a boy two carrels over looked up. She mouthed the rest. To widen the corridor. The throughput. The advantages. She stopped. What were the advantages? Jobs, she guessed, or the city not losing the shipping companies, and she wrote "ventajas" and then nothing under it, because the article hadn't said jobs. She had invented jobs. She crossed it out.

She sat with the crossed-out word for a while. The B2 line wanted advantages and disadvantages of various options, and the article gave her one option, widen and expropriate, and one alternative mentioned in half a sentence, let the companies leave. Rosa Herrera's nets were not an advantage or a disadvantage. Rosa Herrera's nets were a cost that didn't fit in the planner's column, and Isabella did not know whose job it was to say so. Maybe hers. Maybe that was what explaining a viewpoint meant, standing in the gap between the columns.

Dana was watching her. "You're making a face."

"I'm missing something. The article says the companies would go to San Antonio, but it doesn't say what happens to the workers here if they stay. So if I say that's a disadvantage, I'm making it up."

"So say you don't know."

"In Spanish?"

"That's the whole language. 'No se sabe.' That's three words."

Isabella laughed before she could stop it, and the librarian turned from her cart of returns. Isabella lowered her voice. "No se sabe," she said, trying it. The syllables sat more easily than the argument had.

She started over, whispering the summary from the top. The port wanted the houses. The corridor's throughput had to grow. The companies had another option, another port, another city. Rosa Herrera had forty years and a street and an offer that measured neither. "Por una parte," Isabella said, and then, more slowly, "por otra parte." On the one hand. On the other. The scales in the sentence felt honest, like the sentence knew it was leaving something out and was willing to say so. She wrote "no se sabe" at the bottom of her notes and starred it.

Thursday was two days away. Tomas would still roll his r's, and the class would still hear every flat vowel she produced, and she was not sanguine about winning. But the outline hadn't asked her to win. It had asked her to stand there with both hands open, advantages in one, disadvantages in the other, and admit which palm was empty. She read Rosa Herrera's sentence once more, closed the notebook, and slid the article between its pages, the side with the nets facing up.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
Xavier arrived at the library twenty minutes before it opened, which was a kind of asceticism he practiced only during exam week, standing in the cold with his backpack straps gripped in both fists. Inside, he claimed the corner carrel by the window, the one with a wobbly leg he had learned to balance with a folded napkin, and laid out his assignment sheet: a comparison essay on how a parliamentary system chooses and removes a head of government, versus how a presidential one does it. Mr. Okafor had written a single comment in red ink at the bottom. "You have listed facts. Now take a position, and admit what you cannot settle."

The problem was that Xavier did not want to admit anything he could not settle. He liked the clean logic of the parliamentary column: the party that wins seats chooses the prime minister, and if the party withdraws confidence, the prime minister falls, sometimes within days, without any election at all. The presidential column was messier: a fixed term, a direct mandate, removal only through the cumbersome machinery of impeachment, which in his sources had rarely succeeded anywhere it had been genuinely attempted. He copied citations, underlined the word "fusion" where one textbook described the blending of executive and legislature, and felt the pleasing click of a system that seemed to hold together.

"Excuse me. Are you the guy who knows where the law books are?" A girl about his age stood at the edge of the carrel, holding a printed outline with the front page curling. Her name, from the badge on her debate binder, was Priya, and she was preparing a moot court argument against a school dress-code policy, along with two classmates who had scattered toward the computers. "We need the most famous line there is about student speech," she said. "Everyone says it exists, nobody remembers the case."

Xavier almost said he was busy. Then he found himself standing, because the assignment in front of him had begun to feel evanescent anyway, the facts thinning out the moment he tried to build a conclusion on them. He led Priya to the constitutional law shelf and they ran fingers along spines until he pulled a casebook with a battered index. She flipped pages while he read over her shoulder, and there it was, in the section on students and the First Amendment.

"Tinker v. Des Moines," Priya read aloud, slowly, getting each piece into her memory. "1969. The Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." She wrote it down twice, then a third time on her palm. Her teammate Marcus came back from the printers waving a copy and she made him recite the case name back to her, and he got the year wrong twice before he got it right. Xavier watched her insist, and something about her insistence rearranged his thinking more than the textbook had.

He returned to his carrel and looked at his two columns again. Priya's problem had a specific question, a famous line, a ruling, and she was building an argument out of them. His essay had no such spine. He had been trying to compare the systems as though one could be proved better, the way he might prove a math answer, and it occurred to him that political systems were not problems with solutions but arrangements with trade-offs. He took out a fresh sheet and began to contextualize the comparison: the parliamentary system made leaders accountable quickly but made governments unstable; the presidential system made governments stable but let an unpopular leader cling to a fixed term. Both columns were describing the same human difficulty from opposite directions.

He wrote for an hour, crossing out whole paragraphs, then a better hour in which he crossed out less. When he could not decide whether quick removal or fixed stability mattered more, he wrote that down instead of hiding it: that the answer depended on whether one feared disorder more than entrenchment, and that reasonable people in the sources disagreed. His pen slowed at that sentence, because admitting uncertainty felt like a failure, and then kept going, because it also felt, strangely, like the first honest sentence in the draft.

At the study table across the room, Priya's group had begun a practice round, Marcus standing to argue in a voice pitched too loud for the library, Priya leaning over her notes correcting him. A librarian drifted toward them with a look of mild warning, and Xavier watched Priya lower her voice without lowering her intensity, one hand flat on the page where the famous line sat.

On his way out, he stopped beside her. "Which case did you say it was?" he asked, testing her, and himself a little.

"Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969," she said. "Seven to two. Students don't shed their rights at the schoolhouse gate." She tapped the page twice and turned back to Marcus, already arguing again.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Ramadan, many Muslims break each day's fast at the sunset meal, iftar, by first eating a date, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad.
story:
The cemetery sat on a hill above the mosque, which was either planning or happenstance, and Sophie had never decided which. Her grandmother lay under a plain stone near the rowan tree, and it was here, on the afternoon of the ninth day of Ramadan, that Sophie had come to rehearse. In her canvas bag she carried the small notebook where she had written the order of everything: the dates, the water, the maghrib prayer, the food, the tea. Her father had led the family's iftar for as long as she could remember, but this year his shoulder surgery had left his arm in a sling, and he had looked at her across the kitchen and said, "It's yours, Soph. Start to finish."

Start to finish meant the dates had to be ready at the exact moment the sun went down. Not a minute before, not after. She had learned that the hard way two years ago, when she was fifteen and put the dates out early and her little cousin Yusuf, who was seven and fasting his first half-days, had eaten one before the adhan sounded. Her grandmother had not scolded him. She had only looked at the empty space on the plate and then at Sophie, and the look had done all the scolding necessary. Sophie still turned the memory over, the way you keep testing a bruise. She could not decide whether she had failed Yusuf or whether Yusuf had simply been seven, and the wanting had been too much for a small body at sunset.

She sat cross-legged on the dry grass and laid out her supplies like a surgeon. The dates were the recalcitrant ones this year, a box of Medjool from the corner shop, half of them stuck together in a dense brown clump that refused to separate along its natural seams. She worked at them with her thumbnails, splitting the fruit open, easing out the pointed pits, and arranging the halves on her grandmother's favorite plate, the white one with the thin blue rim that she had smuggled out of the kitchen cabinet that morning.

"You're doing it here?" said a voice behind her. Aya had followed her up the hill, which Sophie had neither asked for nor minded. Aya was her cousin and her opposite: loud where Sophie was quiet, certain where Sophie calculated. She flopped down on the grass without ceremony and picked up one of the rejected pits, turning it in her fingers.

"I needed to think somewhere," Sophie said. "And I wanted to ask her."

"Grandma can't tell you the order of an iftar."

"She can, kind of. She did it for forty years." Sophie turned the notebook toward the stone so the pages faced her grandmother's name. "You break the fast with a date first. That's how it's done, the way the Prophet Muhammad did it. Then water, then prayer, then everything else."

"I know that," Aya said, though she said it more softly than she usually said anything.

"I know you know. I'm saying it out loud so it sticks." Sophie separated another date, and its skin tore a little, and she set that one aside for herself, the imperfect one, because she would eat last tonight, after everyone. She had decided that on the walk up the hill, halfway between the bus stop and the gate, and she was still not sure whether it was humility or performance, whether she was serving the family or auditioning for their approval, and she let the not-sure stand. Some things you could hold in both hands at once.

The sun was lowering itself behind the water tower on the far edge of town, and Sophie checked her phone against the paper prayer timetable she had folded into four, because her grandmother had never trusted a phone for this, and Sophie had begun to understand why. The screen said 7:41. The paper said 7:41. The sky said soon. Aya lay back with her hands behind her head and closed her eyes the way fasting people do in the last hour, conserving themselves, and Sophie counted the pitted dates one more time: thirteen for thirteen people, plus the torn one for her, plus one extra laid apart on the grass, in front of the stone.

"That one's for her," Sophie said, without being asked.

"You know she'd say don't waste good dates on the dead," Aya said, but her eyes had gone glassy, and she reached over and straightened the blue-rimmed plate so it sat square to the horizon. The light on the hill turned the color of weak tea, and somewhere below them a door opened and the sound of children spilling out of the mosque reached them faintly, like something fermenting under a lid, pressure building toward release.

At 7:40 Sophie stood, brushed the grass from her knees, and took one date from the plate and held it out to Aya, who took it and stood beside her, and they faced west together where the sun was going down over the water tower, and Sophie whispered, "Okay. Watch the sky. The second it touches the horizon, we eat."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults.
story:
The guidance counsellor's office smelled like instant coffee and the lemon disinfectant they used on the desks between periods, and Hannah had been sitting in the orange chair for eleven minutes because Mrs. Okafor's door was shut and someone was crying in there, audibly, in the way of a person who wanted to be heard through the door.

She had come to drop Calculus. The form was already filled out, folded twice, warm from her pocket. The deadline was four o'clock today; after that she was locked in for the semester, and the semester average she needed for the scholarship was not something she intended to titrate against a unit on integrals. She had done the math. She was good at math, which was the annoying part.

Her phone buzzed. Dev again. can u cover sat? my shift. third time this month. Dev worked the front desk at the rec center with her, had worked it since September, and had developed a talent for discovering, always on a Saturday morning, some obligation that outranked the schedule. He was charming about it, effusive in his apologies, and Hannah had covered twice because the alternative was explaining to their supervisor, whose management style could generously be called autocratic, that Hannah's coworker was a mirage.

The crying in Mrs. Okafor's office stopped. The door opened and a junior Hannah vaguely knew came out with red eyes and a parking pass application, and Mrs. Okafor beckoned her in.

"So," said Mrs. Okafor, reaching for the drop slip before Hannah had fully unfolded it. "Tell me why."

"Calculus is going to wreck my average," Hannah said. "I can take it in college. It's one course. It doesn't matter that much."

Mrs. Okafor didn't answer right away. She was looking something up on her laptop, turning the screen slightly, the way she did when a student's file said something different from the student's mouth. "Your grade is an eighty-one," she said. "That's not wreckage."

"It's going to be a sixty by finals." Hannah sat back. "It's one decision. One semester."

While Mrs. Okafor typed, Hannah's eye drifted to the bulletin board, to a photocopied page pinned between a poster about sleep and a flyer for votech programs. It was a summary of some study, Dunedin, a place in New Zealand, it said, following a thousand people born in one year across their whole lives. An analysis from 2011 had found that children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poorer health, less wealth, and criminal convictions. Hannah read it twice. It did not say how. It didn't say what happened in between the children and the adults, whether anyone had intervened, whether a single dropped calculus course was the same species of thing at all.

Her phone buzzed against her thigh. Dev. please please

"I know what you're thinking," Hannah said to Mrs. Okafor, before the counsellor could say it. "That the small stuff adds up. There's a whole page about it on your board."

"I was thinking about parking," said Mrs. Okafor. "But go on."

"There was this analysis, 2011, of the Dunedin Study. Kids with lower self-control ended up worse off. Health, money, criminal record." She heard herself say it and felt the argument land on her own head like a dropped textbook. "But that's children. Over decades. I'm deciding about one class in one semester. That's different. That's a single, rational, contained decision."

"Is it," said Mrs. Okafor, in the tone of a woman who had filed this exact form four hundred times and could probably predict the date of the final in question.

Here was the thing Hannah could not get around: she liked hard things when she chose them, and she avoided things she hadn't chosen, and Calculus had been her idea until it stopped being fun. Dev, she suspected, was the same. Dev did not think of himself as a person who abandoned his shifts; he thought of himself as a person with extenuating circumstances, each one reasonable, each one single and contained. Whereas the study on the bulletin board said the single and contained decisions were possibly the whole mechanism, or possibly not, since it didn't say, and neither did Hannah.

She picked up her phone. no, she typed to Dev. your shift is your shift. Then she deleted it for something kinder: can't. also you should know the swap list is three people deep and Bev is counting.

"The slip," said Mrs. Okafor, holding out her hand.

Hannah looked at the form, still folded, still warm. Outside, someone's class change rang through the hallway speakers, and she calculated, in the way she calculated, that she had until three fifty.

She tore it in half, once, neatly, and put the pieces in her pocket.

"Wise," said Mrs. Okafor, reaching for her stamp.

"It's one semester," Hannah said. "Ask me in December."

"Ask yourself in thirty years," said Mrs. Okafor, stamping something that was not, after all, her drop slip, and handing her a pass back to class.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2016 ProPublica investigation found that the COMPAS risk tool misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants.
story:
Mr. Okonkwo had divided the class into two benches, and Aidan had drawn the side defending algorithmic bail decisions, which was a problem because he had spent the whole weekend failing to write his opening argument.

"You're overthinking it," Marcus said, sliding into the seat beside him. "It's a debate. You argue whatever side you get."

"I know how debates work." Aidan pulled up his laptop. The classroom's old projector hummed above them, casting a torpid blue wash over the whiteboard, where Okonkwo had written only one word: NEUTRAL. "I just don't believe my side."

"So fake it."

The door opened and Priya came in early, the way she always did, carrying a folder of printed articles because she distrusted screens in arguments. She sat across the aisle and began arranging her pages. Aidan could see headlines upside down, and one of them had a word he recognized from somewhere, COMPAS, though he couldn't place it.

When the bell ended, Okonkwo clapped his hands once. "Computers should decide bail because they are neutral," he read from the board. "Bench one, you defend. Bench two, you dismantle. Five minutes to prepare."

Marcus leaned forward immediately. "Look, a judge has a bad morning, a fight with his wife, he's biased and doesn't even know it. An algorithm never had a bad morning. Same inputs, same outputs. That's your opener."

"That's fine," Aidan said, but he was watching Priya. She had flipped to a specific page and marked it with a yellow tab. He typed into his own laptop, not the debate prep document, just the search bar: COMPAS.

The results loaded and he read the first one twice. He looked up at the clock, which gave him three minutes.

"Bench one," Okonkwo called. "Your case."

Marcus stood. He gave the bad-morning-judge speech, then the part about consistency, then a line about how a tool that treats everyone the same is the definition of fairness. He sat down and nudged Aidan's elbow. "Your turn. Finish strong."

Aidan stood. "I had a second argument," he said. "I don't have it anymore."

"Take your time," Okonkwo said.

"In 2016, ProPublica investigated a risk tool called COMPAS, the kind used in bail decisions." He kept his eyes on Priya, who had stopped arranging her pages. "They found it misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants."

Nobody in the room moved. Someone at the back said, "Twice?"

"About twice the rate," Aidan said. "Same tool, same claim of neutrality." He turned toward his own bench. "I was going to argue that a computer has no volition, so it can't discriminate. But somebody chose the data. Somebody chose what to measure. The neutrality isn't in the machine. It's a claim people make about the machine." He sat down before he could soften any of it.

Marcus stared at him. "You just torched your own side."

"Yeah."

Priya stood slowly. She didn't gloat, which somehow made it worse. "I was going to use the same study," she said. "I spent Sunday deciding whether to say the word COMPAS out loud in this room." She didn't explain why that had been hard, and Aidan didn't ask, though he understood it had something to do with being the only student in the class who would ever have that hesitation.

"Then you agree with me," Marcus said to Aidan, "that the technology is fine and the data is bad? Fix the data, ship the tool."

"I don't know." Aidan heard how weak it sounded and kept going anyway. "Maybe. But we keep hearing that automation removes human judgment, and every example we've studied, the bail tool, the hiring filters, the school surveillance cameras Principal Reyes wants, replaces human judgment with somebody else's judgment, baked in and hidden. At least a judge can be questioned. A score just gets printed."

Okonkwo had been writing on the board through all of this. He underlined NEUTRAL, then crossed the word out, and the dry marker squeaked against the silence. "For Thursday," he said, "you'll each write a position statement. It must contain at least one thing you are still unsure about. I'll fail anything completely certain."

The room emptied in its usual noisy rush, but Priya waited by the door. She held out the yellow-tabbed article. "You should read the whole thing. My printer's dying anyway, so consider it a donation."

Aidan took the folder and slid it into his backpack without breaking it down, the paper stiff against his textbooks. Marcus was already in the hallway calling that he wasn't mad, exactly, but Aidan walked the other way, out toward the parking lot, where the district's new security cameras turned slowly on their mounts above the bike racks, tracking nothing in particular, recording it anyway.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
Jacob stacked the last bag of dark red potatoes, each one smooth and heavy as a lump of igneous rock from the geology unit he'd half forgotten, and looked at the slip of paper in his hand. On it his orientation advisor had written two questions for the small seminar he'd been placed into at State: be ready to explain comparative advantage, and be ready to say why two countries both gain from trading. Three weeks until move-in. He had read the textbook chapter twice on his phone behind the customer service desk, and each time the words dissolved the moment he tried to hold them.

"You're muttering again," said Priya, sliding cartons of eggs onto the belt. She was a sophomore at the community college and had taken the same course, and she enjoyed reminding him of it.

"I'm rehearsing," Jacob said. "Say you're a country."

"I refuse."

"Say you make two things. Say eggs and bread. And say you're actually better than me at both."

Priya scanned a bag of lemons. "Flattering so far."

The register beeped through her answer while he worked it out under his breath. He was better than her at both, yet they still both gained if he specialized in whichever he was comparatively better at. The word wasn't "better." The word was about what you gave up, the loaf you didn't bake. Every time he approached the idea it rearranged itself, and he could feel his advisor's seminar, forty strangers around a table, waiting for him to say something coherent.

An older man came through the lane with a handbasket, banks statements folded inside a newspaper. He asked Priya whether the store had a bulletin board, because he was trying to compare two mortgage offers and kept losing track. He read a line from one sheet, then a line from the other, and shook his head. "The numbers are nothing like when we bought in 2020."

"My mom says the same thing," Jacob said, carrying the man's basket to the end of the lane. "She was at the bank Tuesday. She said the loan officer told her the Federal Reserve started raising its policy rate from near zero in March of 2022 and got it up to between 5.25 and 5.50 percent by July of 2023. She has it written on her hand."

The man frowned at his sheets. "From near nothing to that, in under a year and a half. Different world."

Priya leaned on the register. "Okay, your mom's world, the bank world, the mortgage world, whatever. Get back to your country speech."

Jacob picked up a lemon and a lime and set them side by side on the bagging counter. "Fine. Here. You're the lime country. I'm the lemon country. Say we both grow both." He turned the lemon in his fingers, the oil sharp on his thumbnail. "Say I can grow way more of both. Double the lemons, double the limes. Everyone in my country is better at everything."

"You win."

"Except." He stopped, because the shape of it had finally assembled itself, whole, for the first time. "For every lemon I grow, I could have grown four limes. That's my cost. And for every lime you grow, you only give up half a lemon. So even though I'm better at everything, I'm only really better at lemons, the way that counts. If I grow only lemons and you grow only limes and we trade, there are more of both than if we each did both. Both of us gain. That's it. That's the whole thing."

"Both gain," Priya said slowly. "Even the one that's worse at everything."

"The worse-at-everything country isn't worse at the thing it costs it least to make. That's the point. That's what the chapter kept trying to say."

The man with the mortgage papers had paused at the end of the lane, listening. "So what you're saying is everybody's got something," he said, half to himself, and rolled his newspaper tighter. He said it like a question he intended to carry out to his truck.

Jacob didn't answer right away, because the honest part was still unresolved. His chapter's last page had included critics who maligned the whole framework, who called global trade a machine for plutocracy, a system where the gains from trade pooled at the top while the egg-packing country stayed egg-packing for a generation. He believed both things somehow, that the math held and that the math left people out, and he could not yet say in one sentence where one truth ended and the other began. He would have to say something in three weeks. He could start with the lemons.

Priya picked up the lime and tossed it to him, underhand. "Okay, lemon country. Trade me."

He caught it, cold from the cooler, and held out the lemon in his other hand, and they stood there in the fluorescent hum of lane four, each of them holding the thing the other one wanted.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Justine had written her grandfather's name on the first cup of juice and her own on the second, and now she stood in Aunt Carol's kitchen holding the two cups like evidence in a case she hadn't meant to open. For eleven years Grandpa had led the Seder from the head of the table, and nobody had said out loud that this year would be different, but this year would be different, because he was in the sunroom with a blanket over his legs, dozing before the soup even came out, and her mother had said, quietly, last Tuesday, "You know it. You've watched him your whole life. Just do what he does."

The Haggadahs were stacked by the door, the same battered stack as always, and Justine counted them twice because counting things was what she did when she was about to be responsible for things. At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Her brother Theo was seven now and had been practicing for three weeks, whispering the first question to himself in the bathtub, in the car, once to a cashier at the grocery store who had given him a sticker for it. But Theo got nervous. Theo froze. And when Theo froze, he cried, and when Theo cried, the whole table tilted toward him, and Justine knew, with the certainty of someone who had been an older sibling for seven years, that her first Seder as leader could collapse in the first ten minutes if she didn't plan for it.

"You could just ask them yourself," said her cousin Maya, leaning against the counter, stealing an olive. "You're leading. Nobody would stop you."

"That's not how it works," Justine said. "It's his job. He's the youngest who can."

"So coach him. You're the coach now, apparently. Coach." Maya said the word like it was slightly ridiculous, and it was, and Justine took the olive jar away from her anyway.

The problem was that coaching and leading were two different shapes of attention, and she couldn't be in both at once. If she sat next to Theo and prompted him through the questions, she wasn't at the head of the table holding the order of things together. If she sat at the head, she could see Theo's face going pale from across the room and could do nothing about it. She thought about it while setting the table, while hiding the afikoman under the good napkins, while her mother said, "You're being very quiet," in a tone Justine declined to answer. She was not going to solve it by agonizing. Her grandfather had never agonized; he had improvised. Once, when the candles wouldn't light, he'd declared, "We remember them lit," and everyone had laughed and moved on. Arbitration, that was what he did all night, small rulings on who poured and who read and when the food came, and nobody had ever called it that, but Justine understood suddenly that leadership at this table was mostly just deciding things before anyone had to argue.

So she made a ruling of her own. She put Theo's chair not beside hers but at an angle, close to the head, close enough that she could reach his shoulder without standing up. Then she found him in the hallway, hiding in his dress shirt.

"Here's the plan," she said. "You ask. If you get stuck, I ask the first word of the next line, and you take it from there. Nobody will even notice."

"What if I cry?"

"Then you cry and keep asking. Grandpa mixed up the plagues two years running and nobody fired him."

Theo considered this. "Nobody can fire you if you're grandpa."

"Exactly," Justine said, though this was not exactly what she meant.

Dinner began badly, which is to say it began the way family dinners begin, with her uncle declaring the gefilte fish an abomination and Aunt Carol calling him a philistine and both of them enjoying it thoroughly. When Justine raised her cup for kiddush her voice came out smaller than she'd rehearsed, and she had to start the blessing again, and her ears burned, but the second time was steady, and her grandfather opened one eye from the sunroom doorway and said, "Louder, they're all deaf," which was untrue and helpful.

Then it was time. Theo stood up. His hands found the hem of his shirt. "Why is this night," he said, and stopped, and the table went still in the way tables do when everyone is pretending not to watch. Justine leaned toward him and said only, "different." "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Theo finished, and then the rest came out of him in a rush, all four questions, dipping and reclining and bitter herbs, barely stopping to breathe, and when he sat down he was grinning so hard he looked like he might tip over sideways. Maya raised her glass to Justine from across the table. Justine noticed, at that exact moment, that she had skipped a paragraph in the order of the service, and decided, in the spirit of her grandfather, to fold it in later without announcing the error. She had gained the table and lost the certainty of doing it right, and both of those things were true at once.

Later, after the meal, after her uncle's third monologue about a neighbor whose spending habits he described as profligate, after Theo found the afikoman and held it for ransom with terrifying confidence, Justine went out to the sunroom with a plate of macaroons. Her grandfather was awake, watching through the doorway as she broke the matzah and distributed it.

"You missed the part with the rabbis in Bnei Brak," he said.

"I put it after the meal. Nobody noticed."

"Everybody noticed," he said. "Nobody minded." He took a macaroon and ate it slowly. "Next year, do the rabbis earlier."

"Next year?"

"Next year," he said, and closed his eyes again, and Justine sat beside him and let the evening go on without her for a while.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The municipal pool had the smell of every pool Savannah had ever swum in, chlorine and hot rubber, and a record board so old its letters had the authority of antiquity, times posted by girls who now had children of their own. She read it while waiting for dryland to start, because reading it was easier than looking at Rosa, who had been named putative captain by a vote so close the coach refused to announce the number.

Dryland that Thursday was not dry. Coach Okafor had dragged a battle rope and a thick tow line onto the deck, and after the usual squats he split the team in two and pointed at the deep end gutter, where he had looped the rope through a stainless rail. "Tug of war," he said. "Winners choose the lane order for the relay on Saturday." A cheer went up, thin, because everyone was sore from Tuesday, and Marisol asked whether falling in counted as a forfeit, and he said only for her, which made even Rosa laugh.

Savannah's team lost the first pull in about eleven seconds. She had braced her heels, gripped until her palms burned, and felt, through the rope, a strange softness, as though the other four were holding back a little, saving something, or simply trusting that someone else would take the load. When they regrouped, dripping, Coach Okafor was squinting at them all with the expression of a man doing arithmetic in his head.

"Okay," he said. "New experiment. One at a time. Grip here, pull as hard as you can against the spring scale I clipped to the rail." He held up a rusted spring scale, the kind from a physics classroom, and it turned out the high school would lend anything to anyone who signed a form. Savannah went last. Alone, straining backward against the dial, she watched the needle swing further than it had for anyone else, and she heard Rosa, behind her, say "huh" in a small voice.

The numbers went up on the whiteboard in dripping marker, and then Coach Okafor added a second column, the totals from the group pull divided by five, and the whole deck went quiet in the way a classroom does when something embarrassing becomes visible. Every girl's group number was smaller than her solo number. Every one. "Look at that," Marisol said. "We're a scam." And Savannah, thinking of her psychology textbook, which she read at night the way other people read mysteries, remembered a page she had almost skimmed: a French engineer, Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had people pull a rope and found that each person in a group pulled less hard than the same person pulled alone. She had assumed it was about lazy factory workers in mustaches. It was about her. She said it out loud, carefully, giving the engineer his due.

From where Rosa stood, toweling her hair, the interesting thing was not the scale. It was Savannah's face while she recited the fact, the way she recited everything, like handing over evidence at a trial. Rosa had voted for herself for captain, obviously, and had won or lost by some number nobody would say, and for two weeks she had been waiting to find out what kind of person Savannah actually was. A person who pulled hardest alone, that much was certain now. What Rosa wanted to know was whether such a person could want anything that required other people.

"Okay," Coach Okafor said, "so science says you're all slightly useless together. Excellent. Same teams, pull again, and this time I want you calling your own name when you feel yourself easing off." This was the part he could not abrogate, the ancient rule of Thursday dryland that any drill ending in failure must be repeated until it ended in laughter, and he enforced it with the patience of a man who had run this team for nineteen years.

The second pull lasted a full minute. Savannah called her own name twice, hoarse and ridiculous, and heard Rosa call hers three times, and Marisol once, followed immediately by the slap of Marisol's feet skidding out from under her and the enormous ceremonial splash of a ninety-pound girl entering the deep end fully clothed in a team shirt. Everyone laughed, including Coach, including Marisol from the water, arms spread on the gutter like a woman reclining in a very cold bath. The rope went slack on both sides. Nobody had won. On the whiteboard, in the space for the second pull's totals, someone had drawn a wave.

Saturday, the relay went third. Savannah swam anchor, and when she dove in, trailing by half a body, she thought about the whiteboard and the number that had been smaller than her number, and about Rosa on the second leg lifting her head to call her own name into a silent natatorium, and she could not decide, even mid-stroke, whether the team had taught her to pull harder alone or whether pulling alone had taught her nothing the relay could use. She touched the wall. Somebody's hand was already there. When she pulled off her goggles, Rosa was hanging on the lane line beside her, breathing hard, saying, "Tell me the scale again. I want to write it on my mirror."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew.
story:
Kayla arrived early to philosophy on Tuesday because she wanted the desk by the window, the one where you could hear the radiator ticking and feel slightly outside the room. Mr. Osei had written two words on the board before anyone else came in: unintended consequences. She copied them into her notebook and then, feeling dishonest, underlined them twice.

The problem she carried in with her was a family one, small and specific. Her mother had agreed, over lasagna on Sunday, to pay Kayla's younger brother Devon five dollars per chore, and Devon had gone radiant and cooperative for exactly two days. Kayla had proposed the scheme herself, at the dinner table, as a fair system, fairness being a thing she could defend with arguments. Her mother had set down her fork and said, "In 1902, the French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew." Then she had gone back to her lasagna as though she had said nothing at all. Kayla had spent the night since then being quietly furious, because the story implied she was the kind of person who creates more rats, and because she suspected it might be true.

"Incentives," Mr. Osei said now, walking between the desks. "We reward a behavior and we expect more of it. But what we reward and what we want are not always the same thing. So today, a proposal." He handed a sheet to each row. "The school is considering a new attendance policy. Any student with perfect attendance this term receives a fifty-dollar credit at the campus store. You will argue it in teams, then we will vote."

Kayla's team drew Marcus, who talked like he was being timed, and Priya, who said almost nothing until she had decided something was wrong. They were assigned to defend the policy, which Kayla found convenient and then, on reflection, uncomfortable, because she did believe kids should come to school, and being paid to believe it felt like a corruption she couldn't locate precisely.

"Kids skip because home is bad or school is bad," Priya said, when Marcus had finished a paragraph about responsibility and personal accountability. "Fifty dollars doesn't fix either."

"Nobody's saying it fixes it," Marcus said. "It's a trade-off. We accept imperfect outcomes all the time. Every policy trades something away."

Kayla wrote trade-off in her notebook, next to unintended consequences, and disliked how tidy they looked side by side. She remembered Devon that morning, sweeping the kitchen in a way that moved crumbs from one zone to another so that the counter, his counter, gleamed and the floor got worse. Four days into the system, the chore chart showed a boy in strict compliance with a house that was dirtier than when they started. She had not told her mother, partly because tattling was beneath her and partly because she was still working out whether the dirtier house was Kayla's fault or the system's, and whether that distinction even held.

The debate itself was brief and lopsided. Marcus was fluent and even the opposing team conceded that attendance would probably rise. Mr. Osei called the vote, and it passed easily, and then he said, "One more thing. Beginning Monday, any student who misses a class, excused or unexcused, forfeits the credit." He collected the sheets. "Same policy. One sentence added. Argue with me about it tomorrow."

Walking out, Priya caught Kayla's sleeve at the door. "The sick kids," she said. "The ones who stay home with a fever so they don't infect everyone. The policy maligns them for doing the right thing." Kayla heard her own voice say "exactly" before she had finished thinking it. She pictured the flu moving through the junior class in November, each infected student a small monument to perfect attendance, the credit converting a virtue into an incentive and the incentive back into a harm nobody had voted for.

That night she found Devon on the living room floor, cutting a chore chart out of construction paper, a second chart, subdividing each chore into parts. Dishes would now count as dishes-wash, dishes-dry, and dishes-put-away. He looked up at her with the serene rectitude of a boy who had found the letter of the law and intended to live inside it. "Three chores a night," he said. "Fifteen dollars."

She sat down across from him on the carpet. She had planned to explain the rats again, the way her mother hadn't, and she had a speech half-built about consequences that spread past the moment you stop watching. Instead she said, "What if Mom pays for the week being done, not for each chore? One price. The whole kitchen."

Devon considered it with the gravity of a person renegotiating a treaty. "Then I'd have to do the floor too," he said slowly.

"Right. The floor too." She didn't say that her new system would have its own tail-clipping, some corner she couldn't see yet, some kid at school dragging herself in contagious because fifty dollars mattered more than a fever, and no board, no mother, no sister designing the rules from inside them. She only knew the difference between trying to control an outcome and pretending she could see all of them.

"Fine," Devon said. "But I want it in writing." He slid the construction paper across the carpet toward her, scissors still in his hand.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
Mackenzie locked the bathroom door, set her phone on the edge of the sink, and turned on the fan so her roommate would think she was showering. On the mirror, the steam was already creeping up from the pipes below, and she wrote nothing in it, though she had read somewhere that people did that, in films, to seem decisive.

"Consent is a yes you can take back," she said to the mirror. "A yes for one thing isn't a yes for everything. If someone's been drinking, or they freeze, or they go quiet, that's not a yes." She paused, rewound, started again, and this time the sentences came out level, less like a girl repeating a pamphlet and more like someone who had actually thought about it. Which she had, though not in ways she liked to exhume. There was a night in October, at Devon McCrae's party, when she had said yes to going upstairs and then not said much of anything after, and she had spent months filing that night under things that were probably fine. Probably. She was eighteen now, and the word probably was starting to feel like a debt accruing interest.

Her phone buzzed against the porcelain. A text from Priya: "You've been in there 40 min. Are you alive. Do I need to exhume you."

"Practicing my presentation," she called through the door.

"For peer health training? In the bathroom?"

"It's the only room with a lock."

Priya's voice came closer, warm through the wood. "Then practice on me. I'll be your dumb first-year."

Mackenzie flushed the toilet for cover, then opened the door a few inches. Priya sat down on the hallway floor with her back against the wall, knees up, holding a granola bar like a microphone.

"Okay," Mackenzie said. "Condoms. Every time, start to finish, and yes, for oral too. The pill, if someone's on it, the nurse is obsessed with setting a daily phone reminder, and it's not because she likes notifications. With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. Typical use means real life. Real life means you forget."

"Seven out of a hundred," Priya said. "That sounds low until it's you."

"That's what I keep thinking." Mackenzie looked at her own hands on the sink. She had missed two pills in November, one because of a stomach bug and one because she'd left her pack in a jacket at Devon's apartment, and she had told herself the stomach bug one didn't count and the jacket one was only four hours late. She had never said any of this out loud.

"Next part," Priya said. "Testing. Because that's the part nobody wants to rehearse."

"You don't need an appointment at the campus clinic. You walk in, they ask what you want tested for, and most of it is a urine sample or a blood draw. Chlamydia and gonorrhea can show up in urine. HIV and syphilis are blood. If you have no symptoms they still test you, because most infections don't announce themselves. Results in about a week, through the patient portal, and it's confidential, they won't tell your parents even though you're on their insurance, you just ask billing to keep it off the statement." She ran out of air. "Some infections, like herpes and HPV, need an exam or a swab, so you tell them everything that's happened and they figure out what to check."

Priya was quiet for a second, chewing. "You know you sound like you memorized a manual, right? Which is fine. But you also sound like a person who's about to go to that clinic."

Mackenzie turned off the fan. The silence under it was bigger than she expected. "I missed doses," she said. "Two. And the October thing, the maybe-fine thing. I keep treating that night like it's synecdoche for my whole first semester, like one bad decision stands in for everything I am now, and I know that's a category error, I literally learned that word this week, but knowing doesn't stop it."

"Then don't let it stand in for anything. Go tomorrow. I'll walk over with you and sit in the waiting room doing a crossword like a sagacious old aunt."

"You don't know what sagacious means either, do you."

"Contextually, yes. Like a wise aunt. Same thing."

Mackenzie laughed, then stopped laughing, because her eyes had gone hot without permission. She sat down on the cold tile with her back against the tub, on the same side of the door as Priya now, only the threshold between them. Tomorrow the clinic opened at nine. She had an eleven o'clock class she could miss, or arrive at late, or she could not go at all and keep carrying the word probably around like a stone in her coat pocket, and she understood that both of those futures were fully available to her, and that nobody was going to choose except her.

She picked up her phone and set an alarm for 8:15, labeled it simply with the clinic's address, and turned the screen toward Priya, who nodded once and pushed the rest of the granola bar under the door.

fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
Paige had taped the problem to the inside of her locker door so she would see it between classes: a water balloon launcher on the roof of the gym, a height equation, and the question of the exact angle that would send the balloon the farthest distance before it burst on the parking lot. Mr. Okoye had told the physics club that whoever solved it cleanly would run the launch on Friday, in front of the whole school, and Paige wanted that launch more than she had wanted anything since she'd been cut from the cross-country team in September. The only trouble was that the height equation was a polynomial, and she had never taken a derivative in her life.

She stayed after fifth period in the math lab, a long room of chipped desks where the afternoon light came in sideways and turned the whiteboard into a glare. Devon was already there, working on the same problem, because Devon also wanted the launch. They had been friends since seventh grade and rivals since tenth, and had worked out an arrangement that was less a truce than a habit: they sat at the same table and told each other nothing.

"Do you know what a derivative is?" Paige asked him, breaking the habit within a minute.

Devon kept his eyes on his paper. "It's the slope," he said. "For each term, the exponent comes down and multiplies, and the exponent goes down by one." He slid his notebook six inches toward her, then put his hand flat over the page. "That's all you get."

She copied the rule onto a fresh sheet. Her equation had four terms, the tallest of them an x cubed, and she brought the three down the way Devon had shown her, then the two, then the one, and watched the last term become zero and vanish entirely. What remained was a new polynomial, and she understood, slowly and then all at once, that she was looking at the slope of the balloon's climb, the instant-by-instant steepness of it, and that where that slope crossed zero, the balloon would hang for a fraction of a second at the top of its arc. That was the maximum. She set the derivative equal to zero and solved, and the number she got made her sit very still, because it was the number the whole problem had been hiding.

"I got it," she said, before she could stop herself, and Devon looked up with an expression she could not read.

At home that night she found a message from her sister Ruth, who was a sophomore at a college four hours north and wrote real letters because she claimed texting made her introspect too shallowly. The envelope was thin, and inside was a single page and a photocopied exam. "I lost two marks," Ruth wrote, "and I'm not even angry anymore, but I want you to see it. I left plus C on a definite integral answer. The professor took the marks off without a word. For an indefinite integral you need the constant, because any constant works, so you write plus C to stand for all of them. But a definite integral has limits, real numbers at the top and bottom of the sign. You evaluate at the upper limit and at the lower limit, and the constant is in both answers, so when you subtract the lower one from the upper one, the constant just cancels out. It cancels! It's gone before the end, like it was never there. Two marks, Paige. I've decided to be at peace about it, mostly."

Paige read the letter twice, then sat with the exam copy in her lap, tracing the professor's red circle around her sister's stray plus C. Ruth had put the constant into both evaluations and subtracted, and it had vanished, and Paige felt the odd vertigo of watching something disappear that had seemed, a minute earlier, indispensable. She had been defensive about her own work all week, reactionary almost, snapping at Devon when he looked over her shoulder, treating every question as an ambush. Now she turned her launcher solution over and thought about what in it was load-bearing and what was decoration.

The next afternoon she went back to the math lab early, before Devon arrived, and checked her maximum against the original height equation the slow way, plugging in numbers on either side of the critical value and watching the heights rise and then fall, bracketing the peak like hands closing around a bird. Then she wrote out the whole thing clean: derivative, zero, solve, verify. At the bottom she started to add a constant, because Ruth's habit had migrated into her head, and she stopped with her pen above the paper. This wasn't an integral at all, but she wanted the habit right anyway: constants mattered when they could, and didn't when they couldn't.

When Devon came in, she did something she would have called unthinkable on Monday. She slid her paper across the table to him, all four terms, all her work, the maximum circled in blue. "Check me," she said.

He read it for a long time. His pen hovered, recalcitrant, over her factoring of the cubic, and she felt the old urge to snatch the page back and tell him to fight for the launch like everyone else. She let the urge sit there and exhaust itself. "Your algebra's right," Devon said finally. "Your maximum's right. Mine's different because I set mine up from the parking lot, not the roof."

They looked at each other across the difference, which was, she realized, the actual problem, the one neither of them had been told to solve. Mr. Okoye wanted one launcher, one angle, one clean answer, and the two of them had found two true ones.

"Half each," Paige said.

"I want the last launch," Devon said.

"Then I want the first." She held out her hand and he shook it, quick, like a deal concluded at a market stall, and outside the window the gym roof stood empty and waiting against the cold sky, its launcher still locked in the equipment closet, its angle still, for two more days, undecided.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
Cohen had read the chapter twice before English, and the second time he had done it with a pencil, which meant the margins were now crowded with arrows that pointed at each other. The narrator, a woman named Mrs. Keeling, kept insisting she had married for love, while every detail she offered suggested she had married for the house. Mrs. Abara wanted them to notice how point of view worked on a reader, how the first person invited you in and then quietly picked your pocket. "So is she lying," Cohen asked, "or does she just not know?" Mrs. Abara said that was the question he should bring to his essay, which felt like being handed a box with no bottom.

He wanted the essay to be good, and not only for the grade. His older sister was home from college and had taken to asking what he was reading, and Cohen wanted an answer that wasn't a shrug. The problem was that he could see both sides of Mrs. Keeling. She was either a calculating liar or a sincere woman whose sincerities had been installed by someone else, and he could not tell which essay to write, because each one seemed to cancel the other.

The book club met on Thursdays in the library's back room, an arrangement Ms. Dover had started and then mostly abandoned, so it belonged to the students now. Six of them sat around a table with a scratched surface, arguing about whether Mrs. Keeling's choice at the end, giving up the house to follow a man she barely knew, was courage or something else. Priya said it was obviously freedom, the first real decision in the whole book. Marcus said it was axiomatic that a person can only want what she's been taught to want, and Priya said that was the most depressing sentence she'd heard all year.

"It's not my sentence," Marcus said, and began to gesticulate with both hands, as if the argument were something he could shape in the air. "Simone de Beauvoir. The Second Sex, 1949. She wrote that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Meaning society does the becoming to you. It's on my mom's shelf."

"Fine," Priya said, "but de Beauvoir isn't in this novel."

"That's the point," Marcus said. "She's in the water. She's in every heroine who thinks she chose."

Cohen, who had been peeling the label off his water bottle, stopped peeling. The line Marcus had quoted rearranged the whole problem in his head. If Mrs. Keeling had been made into a certain kind of woman by her society, then her sincerity and her unreliability weren't opposites at all. She could be telling the truth about her feelings and lying about their origin, without knowing either way. The narrator was unreliable not because she deceived but because she reported faithfully from inside a distorted room.

He tried to say this out loud and it came out in three false starts, which Priya let him have, and Marcus interrupted once, and then Cohen got it out whole: "She's not lying to us. She's lying to herself about where her wanting came from, and the book is honest about her dishonesty, if you read the gaps instead of the sentences." The room went quiet in the way that meant people were either thinking or embarrassed for him. Priya said, slowly, that the ending still bothered her, because if everything Mrs. Keeling wants is trained into her, then giving up the house isn't freedom either, it's just new training. Marcus said maybe some wants are more hers than others, and couldn't say how you'd tell.

That was the part Cohen couldn't resolve, and he didn't try to in the essay he wrote that night at the kitchen table. He argued that Mrs. Keeling was a reliable witness and an unreliable guide, and that de Beauvoir's line, which he looked up to make sure Marcus had gotten it right, gave him a way to hold both claims at once. In the last paragraph he admitted the boundary stayed unclear: where the self ended and the shaping began was a question the novel refused to settle, and he had decided to trust the novel's refusal more than his own need for a verdict.

Walking to school the next morning he passed the economics room, where Mr. Vashti was writing "stagflation" on the board for the seniors, a word that meant, as far as Cohen could gather from the grumbling through the door, everything going wrong at the same time. He thought briefly that Mrs. Keeling's world was like that, stagnant and inflating at once, then decided the comparison was clever rather than true and let it go. At lunch he put his essay in Priya's hands and waited while she read the final page. She looked up and said, "You left it open." Cohen said, "Yeah." She handed it back and said, "Good," and went to get in line for the microwave.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: An equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
story:
