His sister had added, "Works on roommates too." Eli didn't know if it worked on best friends you'd known since fourth grade, friends whose flyaway left elbow you'd watched ten thousand times.

The problem was simple and not simple. Marcus had started rushing his second exchange, and at the last meet it had cost them nearly half a second, which in a relay is an ocean. Half a second was the difference between qualifying and watching the sectional final from the folding chairs. Coach had said something vague about "cleaning up transitions," which told Marcus nothing and let him pretend the fault belonged to daylight or the official's whistle. Eli was the one who stood next to Marcus on the line. Eli was the one who could actually see it.

He tried it out in his head during the warmup laps. You're dropping your elbow early. True, specific, useless, because Marcus heard any correction the way he heard his mother about homework: something to be survived. Last season Eli had told him his start angle was off and Marcus had gone petulant for a week, doing the corrected angle with exaggerated slowness whenever he caught Eli watching, a performance of obedience that made them both feel small.

But Eli had also watched Coach Delgado fix a girl on the junior varsity, Priya, whose handoffs had been worse than Marcus's. Coach hadn't softened the criticism. She'd been blunt about the timing, and then she'd said, "I'm telling you because I think you can run with the varsity squad by October." Priya had stopped rolling her eyes at corrections after that. She'd started asking for them. Eli had assumed it was just Priya being mature, but the screenshot made him wonder if the sentence had done something, if belief wasn't a garnish but an ingredient.

Practice divided itself the way it always did, varsity on the near lane, everyone else drifting to the far one, a kind of speciation by stopwatch that Eli usually found funny and tonight found a little sad. He and Marcus were on the same side of it, for now. That was the whole point of telling him. If the elbow kept drifting, they'd end up on opposite sides of the gym, and Marcus would never believe it hadn't been said out of cruelty.

They ran the exchange four times before water break. On the fourth, Marcus rushed it again, the baton slapping into Eli's palm late and crooked, and Marcus's face did the thing it did, the wince he disguised as squinting at the scoreboard clock. Eli walked over with his bottle and made himself start before the silence got too heavy to cross.

"Your left elbow's flying open on the second exchange," Eli said. "You're losing the baton angle, and it's costing us like half a second." Marcus's jaw set, and Eli kept going, faster than he'd planned. "And I'm only saying it because I know you can run a clean exchange. You've done it. I think you're the best sprinter on this team when your form holds."

Marcus unscrewed his cap and drank for a long time. "Half a second," he said finally.

"Half a second."

"Fine. Watch the next one, then. Tell me if it's still ugly." They ran it again, and the elbow stayed tucked, and the baton landed in Eli's palm like it had been aimed there. It could have been the rest between reps. It could have been that Marcus was already tired of rushing. Eli didn't know, and he wasn't going to pretend he did; one clean pass wasn't a study. But at the end of practice Marcus lingered by the door instead of leaving first, and said, "Tomorrow, same thing. If I screw it up, tell me. Don't just tell Coach."

"Deal," Eli said, and picked up both their bags to carry them out.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The printer at the public library charged fifteen cents a page, and Juliette had four dollars in coins, counted twice, in the pocket of her jacket. She logged into the computer by the window and opened her application to Alder College, the school her cousin had gone to, the school with the quiet quadrangle she had visited once in October and thought about every night since. The screen said Early Decision deadline: November 1. Today was October 26.

"You're here again," said Marcus from the front desk as she passed him for more coins. He was a college sophomore on work-study, and he had watched her come in every afternoon that week. "What are you printing, a book?"

"Just forms." She set the quarters on the counter. "One form, a lot of times, because I keep changing it."

"Which school?"

"Alder."

"Early Decision?" He said it the way people name a diagnosis. "You know that's binding, right? If they take you and the financial aid is okay, you have to go. You have to pull all your other applications."

"I know it's binding." She hadn't, entirely, until Tuesday, when she had read the fine print on the agreement three times in a row at this same terminal. The sentence was plain: admitted with acceptable financial aid, she must enroll, and withdraw everywhere else. What the sentence did not say was what counted as acceptable, and that was the part her mother kept circling when Juliette read it to her in the kitchen.

Her mother had two positions and stated both at dinner. The first was that Alder was the place, that Juliette had lit up on that visit, that some things you recognize once and then spend years mistaking for something else. The second was that they had no idea what any school would actually cost them until the offers came, and offers came in the spring, and Alder's estimate was just an estimate. "You can't compare what you haven't seen," her mother said, sliding the salt across the table as though it were evidence. Her uncle, on the phone from Houston, had been more effusive about Alder, calling it an investment, a door, a family standard now that Kaya had gone, and Juliette had felt the pull of that praise and distrusted it in equal measure, because praise cost him nothing.

She printed the form anyway and carried it to the long table near the biography section, where Kaya herself sat across from her, home for the weekend, cracking open a thermos of coffee she was not supposed to have in the building. "So you're doing it," Kaya said.

"I printed the form. That's not the same as doing it."

"Then do it. It's Alder. It's basically yours with your grades."

"Nothing is basically anything." Juliette flattened the page with her palm. "If I apply regular, I hear in March, I get real offers from five schools, and I compare them. If I apply Early Decision, I hear in December, and if the aid is what they call acceptable, I go, and every other application is withdrawn. Done. Before I've seen a single other number." She heard her mother's cadence in her own voice and stopped.

"Kaya, did you apply early?"

"No. Regular. But I wasn't sure about Alder the way you are." Kaya wrapped both hands around the thermos. "That's the difference. You are sure. I watched you on that quad. You looked like you'd been issued a key."

Juliette looked down at the signature line. Two true things sat side by side in her, refusing to merge: that she wanted Alder with a specificity she could not generate for any other school, and that wanting something did not make it affordable, and binding meant betting the whole spring on one school's idea of acceptable. There was a version where she signed tonight and a version where she waited for the March offers, and she could not make either one the obvious one. Waiting felt prudent and also like a small betrayal; signing felt like conviction and also like complicity with a system that asked her to promise before it showed her the price. She noticed her pulse palpitating in her wrist, fast and shallow, the way it did before a race, and she pressed her thumb over it until it slowed.

The overhead lights clicked to half brightness, the library's signal for closing. Kaya capped the thermos. Marcus called out, "Fifteen minutes," from the desk, not unkindly. Juliette folded the form once, then twice, and put it in her jacket pocket, where it sat against the coins, the whole decision now the size of her palm. At the door, Kaya held it open and said, "Whatever you do, do it before the first, okay? Don't let it decide itself." Juliette stepped out into the parking lot and stood a moment under the streetlight, taking the paper out and unfolding it again.

knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
Samuel had the board across two sawhorses in his grandmother's backyard, sanding it down to bare wood by noon. It was a skateboard deck, old and water-stained, that he had bought for five dollars at a yard sale with the intention of turning it into something Dahlia could take to college in the fall. She left in eleven days. He had promised her a deck painted the exact orange of the sunset they had watched from the water tower the summer they were fifteen, that impossible color neither of them had been able to name afterward, though they had tried the whole walk home.

He started with cadmium yellow and added red a drop at a time on a chipped saucer. The first mixtures were promising, warm as toast, and then not warm enough, and then he added more red and it went tomato on him, then rust. He reached for white to lift it back toward light, and the orange dulled immediately, as though he had poured dust into it. He added more red, more yellow, more white, working the brush in small furious circles, and the saucer presented him with brown. Not sunset orange. Brown like the garden soil his grandmother turned over every April.

His grandmother came out with a glass of iced tea for each of them and stood at his shoulder, saying nothing for a while. The chickens muttered along the fence. An autochthonous stand of switchgrass grew up along the back wall, there before the house was, his grandmother claimed, and it moved in the small wind like it knew something.

"It's doing it again," Samuel said. "The brown. It's like it's waiting for me."

"Your grandfather called that color his nemesis," she said. "He painted the porch chairs every spring, and every spring he ended up with a bucket of brown." She tapped the saucer with one finger. "You're mixing everything together. It's subtractive. Every pigment absorbs some of the light, so when you pile them all up, they end up dark and muddy. Never white. The more you add, the less light gets out."

Samuel looked at the saucer. All afternoon he had been thinking of paint as something that added, that accumulated brightness the way words accumulated meaning, and the opposite had been true the entire time. Each pigment was taking something away from the light, quietly, without telling him. "So the sunset color isn't in the saucer at all," he said.

"It might be in the board," she said, and went back inside with her tea, leaving his untouched and sweating on the sawhorse.

He sat with that for a while. His fingers had inured themselves to the smell of turpentine over the summer, so that he barely noticed it anymore, and he noticed it now, sharp, as if his senses were waking up along with the rest of him. He washed the saucer and the brush under the spigot and started over. Instead of mixing, he kept the pigments separate: pure yellow, pure red, pure white, each in its own jar lid. He loaded the brush with two colors at once, barely touching, and drew them across the wood so the yellow dragged thin streaks of red behind it, the red breaking into the yellow like embers. Where the strokes crossed, the eye did the blending from a distance, at the length of a room, the length of a street.

He worked through the afternoon and into the blue hour, when the real sunset began over the roofline, and he held the board up beside it to compare. It was not the same. His orange was rougher, more stubborn, full of visible marks where the water tower sunset had been smooth and vast. But from across the yard, tilted a little, it caught the same temperature, the same refusal to settle into any single name, and he understood that the board would never be a copy of that evening, only a cousin of it, a thing made the opposite way, by keeping the colors apart and letting distance marry them. Whether Dahlia would see the sunset in it or just a nice orange, he could not know, and he found he was all right standing in that not-knowing, brush dripping yellow onto the grass.

He carried the board to the porch and set it on the rail to dry, then stood back from it, arms crossed, head tilted.

"Okay," he said to it. "Hold that."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
The last seat in the lab was by the window, and Camille had habituated to it over six weeks of sitting there, enough that when Mrs. Okafor reassigned the bench groups for the stoichiometry practical, she felt the rearrangement like a small ordinance, something decreed from above and not open to appeal. Her new bench had Priya, who annotated everything in three colors, and Marcus, who had a trenchant opinion on every topic and no patience for anyone else's. Camille wanted one thing from the practical: to leave with a grade good enough to hold her application to the summer research program, which required a B or better in the second semester. Her grade was sitting at a hair above a C.

The task sheet gave them a mass of reactant and asked for the moles of product. Camille read it twice, then a third time, the way you reread a text message hoping it will rearrange itself into sense. Marcus reached for the balance first. "You get the mass. I'll get the mass," he said, though the mass was already printed on the sheet, 4.90 grams of the reactant, and the weighing was only for verification.

"You have to go through the molar mass," Priya said, uncapping a blue pen. "Grams divided by grams per mole, then across the coefficients."

"I know what a mole is," Camille said, and discovered, saying it, that this was only half true. She knew it the way she knew the word for a country she had never visited. She wrote the molar mass of the reactant, 98.09, at the top of her page, then divided 4.90 by it, and the number that came out, 0.0500, sat on her paper looking back at her, small and exact, and she felt something loosen in her chest. One fiftieth of a mole. A countable thing, almost. She looked up the molar mass of the product, 100.46, multiplied, and got a theoretical yield, and then it was Priya's turn with the balance and the filtering flask, and the room filled with the smell of the hot plate warming.

It was while their precipitate was drying that Marcus, flipping ahead in his binder, started the argument. "Next unit," he said. "Equilibrium. Question. If the forward reaction is endothermic, and you warm it up, which way does it shift?"

"Toward the reactants," Priya said. "Heat's on the products' side, so adding it pushes back."

"That's backwards. Endothermic means the forward reaction absorbs heat. So heat it and it goes forward, toward the products."

Priya's pen stopped. "You're treating heat like a reactant. That's not what the question says."

"That's exactly what it says."

They both looked at Camille, the way people look at a third judge, and she wished they wouldn't, because she did not know. What she knew was the small clean chain she had just built, grams to moles, moles to moles, moles back to grams, and it annoyed her that the chain gave her nothing here. She thought about the hot plate in front of them, about their own reaction which had to be kept warm, and she thought about how the teacher had set out two sealed tubes at the front station with a sign that said observe, do not touch, one in an ice bath and one in warm water, both the same reaction, both changing color before their eyes.

"I don't know," she said. "But there's a way to find out that isn't arguing."

The tubes were at the front, and Camille was the one who walked up to them, Priya and Marcus trailing behind. The cold tube held a pale, nearly colorless liquid. The warm tube, the same reaction pushed only by temperature, held a deep, unmistakable blue, the blue of product. Mrs. Okafor had a card beside them with the balanced equation and a single phrase, forward reaction is endothermic, and Camille read it and read the two colors again, the cold faint and the warm saturated, and let the observation settle into the place where Marcus's claim had been standing.

"The products," she said. "If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. The warm tube's the one that went blue."

Marcus made a small sound of vindication. Priya crossed her arms, then uncrossed them, then leaned in to look, and Camille watched her do the thing that honest people do, which is to keep looking after they have stopped wanting the answer to be different. "Fine," Priya said. "But I still think my way of reasoning about it works for exothermic ones. There has to be some version where both framings agree."

"There probably is," Camille said. "I haven't gotten that far." She was aware of how much she hadn't gotten that far on, how the mole calculation had been the first thing all semester to feel like it belonged to her, and how the summer program committee would not care about tubes of blue liquid or about the moment Priya conceded. But when they got back to their bench, the precipitate had dried, and Camille put the filter paper on the balance and read the mass aloud, and Priya wrote it down, and Marcus divided it by the molar mass to compare against her theoretical yield. Their number was low, by about six percent, wet product or lost crystals, and Priya said they should note that, and Camille noted it.

At the end of the period she stayed behind to copy the two tubes into her notebook, the pale one and the blue one, drawing them side by side and writing underneath, warm goes toward the products, endothermic, forward. Mrs. Okafor passed behind her on her way to the ice bath and said, "Next week we do it with numbers."

"Good," Camille said, and kept writing.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech.
story:
The debate packet landed on Violet's desk with a slap that carried through the last rows of Room 214. Mr. Okafor had typed the resolution across the top in bold: the student council should be reorganized as a parliamentary system, its president chosen by and removable by the council's majority vote. Violet's partner, Devon, slid his packet across the aisle and tapped the margin. "We're affirmative," he said. "Easy win. Popularity contest out, accountability in." Violet had learned not to trust Devon's assessments of ease.

The real problem surfaced at lunch. Nia, the student council president, had spent the fall pushing a policy that let students distribute an independent newspaper in the front hall, and Principal Ames had suspended the paper after one issue lambasted the new dress code in language he called inflammatory. Nia had defended the paper publicly, twice, at assemblies. Now three council members were circulating a petition to remove her, claiming she had "lost the confidence of the council." Violet watched Nia across the cafeteria, eating slowly, keeping her face still. "That's a no-confidence vote," Violet said. "That's literally our debate topic." Devon shrugged. "Coincidence. We're affirmative. Use it."

They met Thursday after school in the library's back corner, where the radiators clanked and the windows fogged from the rain. Devon spread his notes: in a parliamentary system, he said, the head of government emerges from and serves at the pleasure of the legislature; a majority can withdraw support and the leader falls. In a presidential system, the chief executive is elected separately, for a fixed term, and can only be removed through impeachment, which is deliberate and rare. He wanted to argue that the first model kept leaders responsive. "So Nia should fall the moment the votes tip," he said. "That's responsiveness." Violet turned her pen over and over. "Or that's a popularity meter. The principal is the one who should be answerable, and he's not even in the equation."

The mock court was the other half of Friday's government grade. Each pair had to argue whether the school could suspend the paper, and Mr. Okafor required them to read the governing text aloud before choosing sides. Devon picked up the handout and read flatly, "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." He looked up. "That's the First Amendment. Ratified in 1791." He said it like a box being ticked, then went back to his notes on Tinker and school publications, building a case that schools could regulate student speech when it disrupted learning.

Violet stopped writing. She read the sentence again to herself, then aloud, slowly, as if the order of the words mattered: "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." "You already read it," Devon said. "Yeah, but you argued from it without hearing it. It says Congress. It doesn't say Principal Ames, and it doesn't say anybody may not abridge speech through pressure, or through a dress code, or through a student council petition." Devon leaned back. "So what, we concede?" "No. We argue the principle and admit the gap. The amendment restrains Congress, ratified in 1791, and everything since has been people fighting over how far it reaches past that one sentence. We can be honest about that and still make our case."

The honesty made Devon uneasy, but Violet pressed him through it. On the walk to the council meeting that evening, the rain gone and the pavement steaming, they drafted the debate position together: parliamentary removal by majority vote makes a leader accountable continuously but vulnerable to faction; presidential impeachment makes removal difficult, which protects independence but can shield a leader from genuine accountability. Violet said the words "I'm not sure which one is better" out loud, and Devon winced, but she kept it in the case. She had stopped being sanguine about easy resolutions; the assignment deserved her actual uncertainty, stated plainly.

The council meeting ran long under the gym's fluorescent glare, folding chairs scraping the varnish. The petitioners moved for a vote on removing Nia. Before the vote, Nia stood and read aloud, from the suspended newspaper's next issue, proofed and printed, the sentence she intended to distribute in the hall regardless of consequence: "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." The room went quiet enough that the radiators could be heard ticking. She said the amendment had been ratified in 1791 and that she was not Congress, and neither was anyone sitting there, and that was exactly why the sentence had to be spoken aloud, over and over, by whoever would speak it.

The vote was eight to seven to keep her. Violet found Devon by the doors afterward. "You still think we should argue she's removable at will?" Devon zipped his bag slowly. "I think we argue both and let the judges squirm." Violet laughed once, short, and folded the handout with the amendment on it into her back pocket. Nia was taping the newspaper to the front hall doors, one strip of tape at a time.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale lists a change in residence as a stressful life event worth 20 points, the same as a change in schools.
story:
Aaron had the moving box on his knees, the one with the ripped corner, and he was holding his phone under it so his father couldn't see the screen. The last message from Dex sat there, unsent: nothing typed yet, just the cursor blinking in the reply field.

"Forty more miles," his father said. "You could look up at the road once."

Aaron looked at the road. Corn, then a water tower, then corn. Somewhere behind the corn was Marcus Hale, who had promised to return Aaron's amplifier before they left, and had not, and now the amplifier was expropriated, legally speaking, by distance. He typed: you still have my amp. He deleted it. He typed: good luck at state. He deleted that too.

"You're doing the thing," his father said. "The thumb thing."

"There's no thing."

"There's a thing."

Aaron put the phone face down on the box. His father's hands were at ten and two, insouciant about nothing, that was the problem; the man drove like the move was a Sunday errand. Two days ago they had loaded the truck in six hours and Aaron had carried his dresser down alone because Dex had a tournament, which was fine, which was understood, which Aaron had said was fine and then thought about for two nights.

He picked the phone back up. He opened a browser instead of the messages, because that felt like work rather than weakness, and he typed: why am i so tired after moving. He expected forums. He got, near the top, a scanned table from something called the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, 1967. He scrolled it the way you scroll anything, half-attending, and then stopped.

"Huh," he said.

"What."

"Nothing." He read it again. Change in residence, twenty points. He checked the next line, sure he had it wrong. Change in schools, twenty. The same. A pair of twenties, listed side by side like the scale couldn't tell them apart. So the tiredness wasn't some private defect; the psychologists had counted it, literally, decades before he was born. Somehow that was the offensive part and the comforting part at once, and he sat with both.

"What's nothing," his father said.

"It's a scale. This psychology thing. From 1967." He angled the screen away without meaning to, then turned it back. "Moving's on it. Changing schools is too. Same points, even. Twenty each."

His father glanced over, one second, then back to the road. "Twenty points," he said. "Out of how many?"

"That part I didn't get to." Aaron scrolled. Death of a spouse was up near a hundred; the whole list ran down through vacations, which had points too, which had to be a typo. He didn't say that part. He said, "It's not the top of the list, is what I'm saying."

"No," his father said. "It's not the top of the list." A mile of corn went by. His father's thumb tapped the wheel twice, then stopped itself. "Your mother wanted to be the one driving you. In case you hadn't figured that out."

"She took the truck with Marcus's mom."

"She took the truck with Marcus's mom so she wouldn't have to watch you not say anything for two hundred miles." His father's voice stayed even, which was how Aaron knew it cost him something. "I drew the short straw. I'm saying it out loud so you know it's a straw and not a preference."

Aaron looked at the box, the ripped corner, his own name in marker on the flap. He understood, abruptly, that his father had been waiting for a conversation the way Aaron had been avoiding one, and that both of them had been counting the miles to something other than a town.

He opened the messages. The cursor blinked. He typed: you'd tell me if the move was harder on you than you act like, right. He read it, deleted "right," put "right" back, and sent it before the second-guessing could arrive. Then he held the phone where his father could see it was a phone and not a wound.

"What's Dex going to say?" his father asked.

"No idea. He's insouciant about basically everything except the triple jump." That got a small exhale from his father, almost a laugh, the first one in three states. Aaron looked up the word phylogeny while he waited, because Dex had used it as an insult last week, something about Aaron's taste in music being an evolutionary dead end, and Aaron had nodded along without knowing. It meant the evolutionary history of a group of organisms. Dex had used it wrong. Aaron screenshotted the definition and sent that too, no caption.

The phone buzzed against the box. Then buzzed again.

"Read it or don't," his father said, "but it's your exit coming up either way."

Aaron read it. The first message said: the amp's in your mom's truck, your dad asked me to leave it with her. The second one said: also it's harder than I act like. obviously. you're the one who never said anything.

Aaron put the phone down on the box, screen up this time, and watched the green sign for the exit rise out of the corn and swing overhead.

"Twenty points," he said.

"Twenty," his father said, and took the ramp.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
The playoff game was at nine the next morning, and the driveway was already losing its light by the time Dez arrived with the ball under his arm and a bag of jersey-wash slung over his shoulder. Luke's backyard hoop had a bent rim from the winter his cousin had hung on it, and the free throw line was a chalk mark that rain had softened into a ghost. It was the only court they had since the rec gym got double-booked for a craft fair, and it would have to be enough.

"Ten minutes of warm-ups," Luke said, "then we run the offense."

Dez dribbled twice, stopped, and looked at him with the particular seriousness he saved for strategy. "New rule tonight. Whoever hits three in a row, we feed him. Ride the hot hand. Coach would've said the same thing."

Coach Okafor had been reassigned by his company to a branch in Dallas on Thursday, which was how Luke, a sixteen-year-old with a bent rim, had become the person responsible for their half-court sets. He hadn't asked for it. He wasn't sure he wanted it. But the game would happen whether he was ready or not, and there was something clarifying in that, the way a deadline strips a problem down to what you can actually solve before dark.

They ran the offense. Dez was good at it, honestly, a connoisseur of passing angles, the kind of player who noticed where the help defense was drifting before it started drifting. But every few possessions he would stop the movement and force the ball toward whoever had just made shots, even when that person was Marcus, whose idea of footwork was a small hopeful hop. Twice Marcus traveled. Once he threw the ball over the fence into the Hyatts' tomato cages.

"Did you see that?" Dez said, retrieving it. "He was feeling it. Three straight. You don't take the ball out of a shooter's hands when he's feeling it."

Luke had his doubts, and he didn't yet have anything to back them with except a general unease, a sense that Marcus's made baskets and Marcus's next shot might not be connected the way Dez believed. He remembered his father's study, the shelf of old paperbacks with cracked spines, one of them a collection of writing about thinking, about how people see patterns. He'd flipped through it once and put it back. Now, while the others did layups, he went inside and found it and thumbed through the index, and there it was, a chapter on randomness and sports.

He read it standing by the kitchen window, one eye on the backyard. In 1985, three researchers, Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky, had studied the shots of basketball players and concluded that a shooter's streaks were no more common than you would expect from chance alone. The paper called the hot hand a fallacy. Luke read the sentence twice, then a third time, and felt something shift in him, the way a room looks different after you learn what a wall used to be. All those years of announcers shouting about a player being on fire, and the numbers said the fire was, at least in that study, an illusion.

He carried the book outside. "Listen," he said. "One experiment, then we go back to drills."

Dez crossed his arms. "We got a game at nine."

"Exactly. Twenty minutes." Luke found a golf pencil in the garage and an old spiral notebook with a water stain shaped like Ohio. "Everybody shoots twenty free throws. We write down makes and misses in order. Then we look at what happened right after three makes in a row. If the hot hand is real, they should hit more often after three makes. If it's the fallacy, they'll hit about their normal rate."

"It's called the hot hand fallacy?" Marcus asked, squinting at the page.

"That's what the study called it," Luke said. "I'm not saying it's the whole truth. I'm saying let's look."

The light went amber and then gray while they shot. The chalk line turned soft under their sneakers, and the ball's thump against the bent rim kept a stubborn rhythm, and mosquitoes came up from the ivy along the fence. Dez was the best shooter, which everyone knew, and he made fourteen of twenty, but after his runs of three makes he clanked the next one more often than not, and when they counted, his percentage after streaks came out almost exactly his overall percentage. Marcus, who made six of twenty, hit two in a row once and missed his next three. JJ's numbers wobbled small and meaningless, like weather.

"So it's fake," Dez said, but he said it slowly, and he was looking at the notebook, not at Luke.

"I don't know that I'd go that far. One driveway, one evening, forty free throws total." Luke tapped the page. "The study was real, and it was bigger than us. But it doesn't mean you never pass to a guy who's made three. Maybe confidence changes something the study couldn't see. Maybe what it changes is how hard he tries on defense, or how the other team guards him." He paused, hearing himself stack maybe on maybe, and decided he was okay with the stack. "What I think is this. You pass to the open man. If the open man happens to be hot, great. But we don't force it to Marcus just because he made three and everybody's yelling."

Dez was quiet for a moment, and it didn't seem like sulkiness; it seemed like a person watching an old idea get taken apart to see if it still worked. He'd always hated when other teams denigrated their rec league, called it pretend basketball, and Luke knew that underneath the trash talk Dez actually wanted the game to make sense, to have laws, to reward the people who understood it best. "All right," Dez said finally. "Open man gets the ball. But if I hit three straight tomorrow, I'm calling for it anyway."

"Call for it," Luke said. "I'll still throw it to whoever's open."

They ran the offense until they couldn't see the rim, just the pale square of the backboard and the darker blur of the ball moving through it, and Dez threw a no-look pass to JJ in the corner that JJ buried, and nobody on the whole dark court had made three in a row. "Again," Luke said, backing out to the chalk ghost with the notebook still under his arm.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Selected Works section asks for 5 artworks and counts for 40 percent of the score.
story:
The art shack at Camp Wenonah smelled of turpentine and bug spray, and by four o'clock on the last full day, Elijah had spread his portfolio across two picnic tables pushed together, sixteen pieces he'd made over three summers, drying in the heat like evidence at a trial he was losing. He had until the evening showcase to submit his AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio, or rather to submit what he could of it, because the deadline the College Board would not extend was the same deadline the camp bus would not delay, and the cabin wifi reached only as far as the picnic tables, barely.

"You're doing the Selected Works section?" said Priya, dropping onto the bench across from him with her own stack of charcoal drawings. "How many do you need?"

"Five," Elijah said. "And the whole section's only worth forty percent of the score." He said it flatly, the way you report a sentence you've already served.

Priya whistled. "So which five?"

That was the problem. He had a still life with a broken mirror, two self-portraits, a color study of his mother's kitchen, a copy exercise of Hopper's light, and half a dozen others, and no principle for choosing among them beyond liking them, which he distrusted, because liking was how he'd chosen everything so far, including this camp.

The art instructor, a taciturn man named Mr. Okonkwo who mostly painted watercolors of the lake and spoke maybe forty words a day, had left a single book on the table that morning: a monograph of Frida Kahlo, with a sticky note on the self-portrait with thorn necklace and hummingbird. "For the written part," was all he'd said.

Elijah opened it now, mostly to avoid his own work. The hummingbird, black and dead, hung at the throat. The thorns drew a line of blood down the neck and chest. Background leaves pressed forward, flat and crowded, closing in, while the face stayed perfectly still, composed, almost serene. He'd seen the painting before, in a textbook, and had done the thing he suspected everyone did: felt something large and vague and moved on. But the written portion of his portfolio asked for analysis, not feeling, and he didn't know the difference yet, or whether there was one.

"She looks calm and it's a lie," Priya said, leaning over.

"Or she looks calm and it's the truest thing in it," Elijah said. He turned the page and back. The leaves were the same green as the parrot in the background foliage, almost the same green as her shawl wasn't. The blood was red, precise, small. Nothing in the painting was accidental; every color had been placed, which meant every color could be discussed. "Look at the composition. Everything pushes in on her. The animals, the plants. But she's the vertical. She holds."

"Is that analysis or is that you liking it?"

He didn't answer, because the question was a good one. He took out the notebook where he'd been drafting his portfolio statement and started writing instead: the saturated greens compress the space; the hummingbird, a symbol of fallen warriors in Aztec tradition, hangs dead at the throat like a pendant; the symmetry of the face against the asymmetry of the blood. He wrote fast, and the sentences came out more certain than he felt, which bothered him, and then didn't, because he was running out of afternoon.

"Five pieces," Priya said again, tapping his still life with the broken mirror. "This one, obviously."

"Why obviously?"

"The mirror. It's doing what the thorn necklace does. Showing the wound as an object."

He looked at the still life, at the fracture running through his own painted reflection, and realized he'd been trying to litigate the choice piece by piece, each artwork pleading its case, when the actual question was what the five said together. A portfolio wasn't five best pieces; it was one argument in five parts. He pulled the two self-portraits forward, the color study of his mother's kitchen where the yellows did something he'd never been able to name and could now almost name, and, after a long moment, the Hopper copy, because light was a subject too and he could defend it.

"That's five," Priya said. "You're sure?"

"No," he said. "But I can say why I picked them, and yesterday I couldn't." It came out sounding smaller than it felt. The gain had a cost he was aware of: in learning to see the paintings as formal objects, color and composition and symbol, something had loosened between him and them, some unmediated pleasure he wasn't sure would come back. He could analyze the thorn necklace now, and quote the hummingbird's meaning, and he would never again stand in front of it the way he had at sixteen, before he knew anything, when it had simply gone through him like weather.

He photographed the five pieces in the slanting light, checking each image against the actual painting for veracity, because a smudge in the photo would count as a smudge in the score. Priya held the reflector, an overturned cafeteria tray wrapped in a white T-shirt. Somewhere across the field the dinner bell rang, then the bus horn, early, the way it was early every year when the counselors wanted to swim before dark.

Mr. Okonkwo came up the path as Elijah hit submit on the last upload. He looked at the open Kahlo book, at the notebook, at the five paintings now stacked and tied with the ribbon from Priya's hair. He picked up the notebook and read the line about the hummingbird, the pendant, the symmetry, and his face did something Elijah had never seen it do.

"Hopper copy," Mr. Okonkwo said finally. "Brave or stupid. We'll find out in July."

"Which do you think?"

Mr. Okonkwo handed back the notebook and picked up his watercolors, already half packed, and started down toward the lake where the light was going gold and wrong in the way painters wait all summer for.

Elijah closed the Kahlo book and put his thumb on the dead hummingbird for a second, then slid it into his duffel with everything else.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: An 'I-message', popularized by psychologist Thomas Gordon, states the speaker's own concern, such as 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline', instead of accusing the listener with 'you' language.
story:
Joseph considered himself the most patient person at the Harvest Table volunteer office, which was easy to believe on a Tuesday afternoon when the filing was done and the only sound was the hum of the old refrigerator. He sat at the front desk with the sign-in binder open in front of him, and the numbers there told a story he did not like. Every Thursday for six weeks, Renata had clocked out at 5:40 instead of 6:30. Somebody had to re-shelve the pantry boxes alone, and lately that somebody was him.

He was not angry, he told himself. He was concerned, in a professional way, the way the coordinator Ms. Okafor was concerned when grant reports came in late. He wanted to write that down, actually write it, because the office had a rule that shift concerns went through the message board tacked beside the refrigerator, and Ms. Okafor had said twice that she liked structured notes better than hallway complaints. So Joseph sharpened the good pencil and began a draft.

"Renata, you keep leaving early and you never tell anyone," he wrote, and then, because it sounded harsh, "You are being inconsiderate to the whole team." He read it back and felt a small clean satisfaction, which should have warned him. Instead he drifted into a brief reverie, imagining Ms. Okafor reading the note aloud at the monthly meeting, nodding, maybe promoting him to shift lead.

"Too doctrinaire," said Priya from the donations table, leaning over his shoulder without apology. She was seventeen and read everything, including other people's drafts. "You sound like a rulebook with a grudge. She'll read two lines and stop."

"It's structured," Joseph said. "It's professional."

"It's an accusation sandwich." Priya flipped the binder to the staff resources shelf, pulled down a thin book by a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, and dropped it on the desk. "Look at the middle part."

The middle part had a heading about I-messages. Joseph read it twice, slowly. An I-message, the page said, stated the speaker's own concern, something like "I'm worried we'll miss the deadline," instead of accusing the listener with "you" language. He looked at his draft, where the word "you" appeared four times, each one like a pointed finger.

"That's the whole trick?" he said. "Say I instead of you?"

"That's the whole trick," Priya said, and went back to sorting cans of chickpeas.

Joseph tore up the first draft, which he would later describe as a calm revision rather than what it was, and wrote a second. He kept it short and structured, a subject line, the dates, the concern, a question. Then he copied it onto the message board, where the whole office could see it, which felt brave and slightly sickening.

The board note read:

To Renata, re: Thursday shifts. I've noticed the last six Thursdays have ended at 5:40 instead of 6:30. I'm worried the pantry boxes won't get shelved before the Friday distribution, since I can't always stay late. If something is going on with your schedule, could we talk about covering it differently? I'd rather sort it out than let it build. Joseph.

He went home feeling like a diplomat. He told his brother he had handled a workplace conflict with emotional maturity, and he half believed it, except for the part of him that had wanted, faintly and dishonestly, for Renata to feel stung.

Thursday came. Renata arrived at four with wet hair and a hospital parking sticker on her jacket. She read the board note standing up, one hand on the refrigerator door, and then she turned around.

"My mom has dialysis Thursdays at six," she said. "The clinic is twenty minutes away. I've been telling Ms. Okafor I had to leave, but I never put it on the board because it felt like asking for special treatment. I thought I was being discreet." She paused. "Your note is the first time anyone said it in writing where I could answer it in writing."

She took the good pencil, which was hers anyway, and wrote below his note: "Joseph, thanks for saying it as a concern instead of a complaint. I'll ask Priya to shelve Thursdays, and I'll take her Saturday morning slot. Also, I can stay this Thursday, my mom's appointment moved to Friday."

Joseph read it standing where she had stood, one hand on the refrigerator. The patient diplomat, the office peacemaker, had spent six weeks shelving boxes alone and never once asked her why, because asking would have meant discovering that the problem was not inconsideration but information, and that the person who never communicated anything in writing had been, all along, him. He picked up the pencil to write one more line, and beneath her words he printed, slowly: "I should have asked sooner. My fault, not just the schedule's."
